PROPOSED EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

1. Identification Strategy  
I will use an instrumental-variables (IV) difference-in-differences (two-way fixed-effects) framework.  
• Outcome: Central-city population (levels or logs).  
• Endogenous regressor: the stock of limited-access “rays” reaching the CBD.  
• Instrument: the number of rays implied by the 1947 interstate blueprint (“planned rays”), interacted with decade dummies.  
Why IV?  Actual urban highway construction after 1950 was partly driven by local commuting demand and therefore endogenous to population trends.  The 1947 plan, however, was drawn up before post-war suburbanization, emphasised inter-regional connectivity, and was adopted before large federal construction funds existed (1956).  Using it as an instrument isolates the component of highway supply that is plausibly exogenous to subsequent within-metropolitan residential sorting.  
The DID/time-FE dimension comes from panel data across MSAs and decades (1950, 1960, … 1990).  MSA fixed effects control for time-invariant local attributes; decade fixed effects absorb nationwide shocks (e.g., baby boom).  

2. Treatment and Control  
• Treatment variable (continuous): Rays_it – count of limited-access highway segments whose centerline passes ≤1 mile from the 1950 CBD of MSA i in decade t.  
• Instrument: PlannedRays_i × Decade_t, where PlannedRays_i is the count that the 1947 map would have delivered to MSA i.  
• Control: Identification relies on cross-sectional variation in PlannedRays_i.  MSAs with few or zero planned rays serve as the counterfactual for those slated to receive many, after netting out MSA and decade fixed effects.  
• Timing: Treatment “starts” once construction enters the urbanized area.  We operationalise this by decade: Rays_1960 is the stock opened by 1 Jan 1960, etc.  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1 (Relevance): PlannedRays_i strongly predicts actual Rays_it after 1950.  Plausible because 85-90 % of planned mileage was built and route locations were fixed early.  
A2 (Exclusion): Conditional on MSA and decade fixed effects plus controls, PlannedRays_i affects central-city population only through the highways that were actually built.  Plausible because the blueprint emphasised national defence and inter-city freight corridors, not local commuting patterns.  
A3 (Smooth Trends): In the absence of new highways, MSAs with high vs. low PlannedRays_i would have experienced parallel central-city population trends.  We will probe this with pre-trend tests (1940-50).  
A4 (Stable Unit Treatment): Highway construction in one MSA does not directly affect populations of other MSAs (reasonable at the metropolitan level).  
A5 (No Differential Measurement Error): Highway counts and population measures are comparably accurate across MSAs and decades.  

4. Main Threats and Mitigations  
T1 (Local endogenous add-ons): States/cities sometimes built additional urban expressways beyond the federal backbone, possibly responding to depopulation.  
 Mitigation:  First-stage isolates the exogenous blueprint component; including controls for state gasoline‐tax revenue, state political variables, and decade-state FE further absorbs endogenous state road spending.  
T2 (Planned route placement correlated with 1940 characteristics that also forecast depopulation—e.g., industrial structure).  
 Mitigation:  Control for 1940 log MSA population, simulated mean household income, 1940 industry‐skill‐mix variables, 1940 Gini, and weather; include pre-trend falsification (1930-40, 1940-50) to detect anticipatory divergence.  
T3 (Spatial spillovers within multi-city MSAs): Interstates might steer population from the largest to smaller central cities inside the same MSA.  
 Mitigation:  Redefine outcome using the 1950 central‐city boundary (constant geography) and, as robustness, total population within 5 mi, 10 mi, and 15 mi rings around the 1950 CBD.  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast TWFE and IV
library(did2s)       # for event studies
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data
dt <- fread("msa_panel_1950_1990.csv")  # One row per MSA–decade

# 2. Variable construction
dt[, ln_cc_pop  := log(cc_pop)]                 # outcome
dt[, decade     := factor(year)]                # 1950 = base
dt[, ln_msa_pop := log(msa_pop)]
# First stage vars
dt[, rays       := urban_rays]                  # actual stock
dt[, planned    := planned_rays]                # from 1947 map
dt[, instr      := planned * as.numeric(decade)]# interacted IV

# 3. Main IV TWFE regression
iv_main <- feols(ln_cc_pop ~ rays | msa_id + decade | 
                 (rays ~ instr), data = dt,
                 cluster = ~msa_id)
summary(iv_main)

# 4. First-stage F-statistic
wald(iv_main, "fit_rays = 0")   # relevance check

# 5. Pre-trend test (1930-50)
pre <- feols(ln_cc_pop ~ planned*year | msa_id + year,
             data = dt[year %in% c(1930,1940,1950)])
summary(pre)

# 6. Event-study illustration
es <- did2s(dt, yname = "ln_cc_pop", first_stage = FALSE,
            treatment = "rays",
            idname = "msa_id", tname = "year",
            xformla = ~ ln_msa_pop + weather + mean_inc_1940)
plot(es)

# 7. Robustness: drop coastal MSAs
iv_inland <- feols(ln_cc_pop ~ rays | msa_id + decade | 
                   (rays ~ instr), data = dt[inland==1],
                   cluster = ~msa_id)
etable(iv_main, iv_inland)
```

6. Expected Results  
Economic intuition suggests that additional highway rays facilitate commuting from suburbs to the CBD, lowering the relative price of suburban residence and encouraging decentralization.  I therefore expect:  
• Direction: Each extra ray reduces central-city population (negative β).  
• Magnitude (rough prior): A back-of-the-envelope elasticity of –0.03 to –0.05; e.g., adding two rays (≈ one standard deviation) would lower central-city population by 6–10 %.  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)  
C1: Strong first stage (F > 10) …………………… 1  
C2: Exclusion plausibly holds given 1947 plan … 0.7  
C3: No differential pre-trends …………………… 0.8  
C4: No spillovers/interaction across MSAs …… 0.7  
C5: Correct functional form & clustering ……… 1  
Average ≈ 0.84 → Method reasonably credible but not bullet-proof.
